holding: C.P.L.A.No.3740/2019 arising out of the same impugned judgment and involving identical questions of fact and law, was heard together with the present appeal. Since the issues raised therein stand fully covered by the reasons recorded above, the said petition is disposed of in the same terms.

paragraphs.text: SHAHID BILAL HASSAN, J- Brief facts germane to the filing of the instant appeal are as such that agricultural land measuring 66 Kanals and 01 Marla situated in Mauza Langar Pakhral, Tehsil Sohawa, District Jhelum, was transferred in favour of the appellant through Mutation No.408 dated 15.07.2002. The respondents’ predecessor-in-interest, Nazar Muhammad (“pre-emptor”), asserted that the sale had been affected in favour of the appellant for a consideration of Rs.198,000/-. It was further alleged that on 07.10.2002 at about 9:00 a.m., the pre-emptor received information regarding the sale from one Javed Hussain in the presence of Karam Hussain, whereupon he immediately performed Talb-i-Muwathibat and thereafter dispatched notice of Talb-i-Ishhad on 08.10.2002. On the basis of the aforesaid assertions, a suit for possession through pre-emption was instituted on 11.11.2002. The appellant contested the suit through a written statement, denying the allegations and specifically disputing the lawful performance of Talbs. Upon completion of pleadings, issues were framed and the parties led evidence in support of their respective claims. After evaluating the material available on record, the learned trial Court, vide judgment and decree dated 01.12.2006, held that the pre- emptor had successfully established the performance of Talbs. Nevertheless, the suit was dismissed on the ground that the pre- emptor had failed to establish a superior right of pre-emption vis-à- vis the appellant. Aggrieved thereof, the respondents preferred an appeal before the learned Additional District Judge. The learned appellate Court, vide judgment and decree dated 13.03.2010, concurred with the findings of the learned trial Court regarding performance of Talbs but disagreed with its conclusion concerning the respective rights of the parties. Holding that both the appellant and the respondents were co-sharers in the Khata, the learned appellate Court partly decreed the suit and granted pre-emption to the extent of fifty percent of the suit property. Both parties felt dissatisfied with the appellate judgment. Consequently, the appellant filed Civil Revision No.315-D of 2010 before the Lahore High Court, whereas the respondents instituted Civil Revision No.360-D of 2010. By means of the impugned judgment dated 13.06.2019, the learned High Court dismissed the appellant’s revision petition and allowed the respondents’ revision petition. The learned High Court held, inter alia, that the findings regarding performance of Talbs had attained finality; that the plea regarding limitation was without substance; that the right of pre- emption survived the death of the original pre-emptor and devolved upon his legal heirs under section 16 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1991; and that the appellant had failed to establish his alleged co- sharership in the Khata. Consequently, the respondents’ suit was decreed in its entirety. Hence, the present appeal is before this Court.

Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the judgments rendered by the Courts below suffer from patent misreading and non-reading of evidence and are contrary to the settled law governing pre-emption. He argues that the plaint does not contain the mandatory particulars relating to Talb-i-Muwathibat, namely the precise date, time and place of its performance, rendering the suit legally incompetent from its inception. According to the learned counsel, such omission is fatal in view of the law consistently declared by this Court in a long line of authorities. Learned counsel further contends that the respondents failed to establish the complete chain through which information regarding the sale allegedly reached the pre-emptor. He submits that neither the pleadings nor the evidence disclosed the source from whom the alleged informer acquired knowledge of the transaction. According to him, the omission strikes at the very root of Talb-i- Muwathibat and is fatal in view of the principle enunciated by this Court in Muhammad Riaz v. Muhammad Akram and others (2024 SCMR 692). Learned counsel also submits that the notice relied upon as constituting Talb-i-Ishhad does not contain any confirmation or reiteration of the intention to exercise the right of pre-emption as required by section 13(3) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1991. He argues that mere dispatch of a notice, without strict compliance with the statutory requirements, does not amount to valid performance of Talb-i-Ishhad. Lastly, learned counsel submits that the learned High Court completely overlooked the admissions made by PW-4, PW-5 and PW- 6 regarding the appellant's co-sharership in the property and, therefore, illegally interfered with the findings recorded by the learned appellate Court on that issue.

Conversely, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents supports the impugned judgment. He submits that the Courts below concurrently found that the Talbs had been validly performed and that such findings are based upon proper appreciation of evidence. According to him, the objections raised by the appellant are hyper-technical in nature and do not affect the substance of the respondents’ claim. He further contends that the appellant failed to establish his alleged co-sharership and that the learned High Court rightly corrected the error committed by the learned appellate Court.
We have heard the learned counsel for the parties at length and have examined the record with their able assistance.

The controversy in the present appeal essentially revolves around whether the respondents successfully established, in the manner required by law, the performance of the mandatory Talbs constituting the foundation of a claim for pre-emption. This necessitates examination of several interconnected questions, namely, whether the plaint contains the essential particulars relating to Talb-i-Muwathibat; whether the respondents proved the complete chain through which information regarding the impugned sale reached the original pre-emptor; whether the evidence concerning the alleged Majlis and performance of Talbs is free from material contradictions; whether Talb-i-Ishhad was performed and proved in accordance with the statutory requirements; whether the learned High Court was justified in declining to examine the legality of the Talbs on the ground that no cross-objection had been filed against the findings of the learned trial Court; and whether the learned High Court lawfully interfered with the findings of the learned appellate Court regarding the appellant's status as a co- sharer in the suit property.

Before examining the evidence available on record, it would be advantageous to revisit the settled principles governing the right of pre-emption. It is by now well-established that the right of pre- emption is not a right to acquire property in the ordinary sense but a right of substitution, whereby the pre-emptor seeks to displace a completed sale and step into the shoes of the vendee. Owing to its very nature, the right has consistently been described by this Court as a weak, feeble and fragile right, capable of defeating a lawful transfer of property only when every statutory requirement prescribed for its exercise is strictly complied with. Consequently, a claimant, seeking enforcement of such right, must plead and prove the same as required by law, as any deficiency in respect thereof is fatal to his claim.

The statutory scheme embodied in section 13 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1991, recognizes three demands, namely Talb-i- Muwathibat, Talb-i-Ishhad and Talb-i-Khusumat. Of these, Talb-i- Muwathibat occupies a position of paramount importance, for it constitutes the very foundation upon which the subsequent demands are built. It is only after the pre-emptor acquires knowledge of the sale and immediately asserts his intention to exercise the right of pre-emption through Talb-i-Muwathibat that the obligation to perform Talb-i-Ishhad arises. Failure of the foundational demand necessarily renders all subsequent acts legally inconsequential.

The law on the subject was authoritatively settled by a five- member Bench of this Court in Mian Pir Muhammad and another v. Faqir Muhammad through L.Rs. and others (PLD 2007 SC 302). After reviewing the entire jurisprudence relating to pre-emption, the Court held that a pre-emptor is under a legal obligation to specifically plead the date, time and place of Talb-i-Muwathibat as well as the particulars relating to Talb-i-Ishhad. This Court approved the principles earlier enunciated in Haji Muhammad Salem v. Khuda Bakhsh (PLD 2003 SC 315) and Fazal Suhhan and others v. Mst. Sahib Jamala and others (PLD 2005 SC 977) and declared that omission of these foundational particulars is fatal to a suit for pre- emption.

The rationale behind the rule is not difficult to discern. Talb- i-Muwathibat is commonly understood as a "jumping demand", that is to say, an immediate and spontaneous assertion of the right of pre-emption the moment knowledge of the sale is acquired. The law insists upon strict pleading of the date, time and place of such demand because only then can the Court determine whether the demand was made instantly and without avoidable delay. These particulars are therefore not matters of form but matters of substance going to the root of the claim. If the foundational demand itself is not properly pleaded, the Court is deprived of the ability to examine whether the statutory requirement of immediacy has been fulfilled.

The aforesaid principle has been consistently reaffirmed by this Court. In Khyber Khan and others v. Haji Malik Amanullah Khan (2007 SCMR 1036), it was held that omission to mention even one of the three essential particulars—date, time or place—of Talb-i- Muwathibat is sufficient to defeat the claim. Likewise, in Dr. Pir Muhammad Khan v. Khuda Bakhsh (2015 SCMR 1243), this Court reiterated that strict adherence to the requirements governing Talbs is indispensable. More recently, in Farid Ullah Khan v. Irfan Ullah Khan (2022 SCMR 1231), it was observed that Talb-i-Muwathibat constitutes the very foundation of the right of pre-emption and where such demand is not proved in accordance with law, the entire superstructure collapses.

The same view was reiterated in Sardar Muhammad (deceased) through LRs v. Taj Muhammad (deceased) through LRs and others (2023 SCMR 1113), wherein this Court held that a pre- emptor must not only plead but also prove the valid performance of Talb-i-Muwathibat and Talb-i-Ishhad, and that failure to establish any one of the statutory demands is fatal to the suit. Similar observations were made in Kashmali Khan and others v. Mst. Malala (2023 SCMR 1176), where it was emphasized that because pre- emption is a weak and feeble right, every requirement relating to Talbs must be observed with utmost strictness.

Very recently, in Ghulam Abbas v. Abdul Sattar and another (2026 SCP 172), this Court revisited the entire jurisprudence relating to Talbs and held that the requirement of specifically pleading the essential particulars of Talb-i-Muwathibat is not a mere technical formality but is intrinsically linked to the statutory scheme governing pre-emption. The Court further held that where the plaint itself does not disclose the mandatory particulars of the demand, the claim becomes legally deficient at its inception and no amount of evidence subsequently led can cure the defect.

Assuming for the sake of argument that the pleadings were sufficient, the respondent(s) were still required to establish through cogent, confidence-inspiring and legally admissible evidence that the original pre-emptor acquired knowledge of the sale in the manner alleged and immediately exercised his right through Talb-i- Muwathibat. The requirement assumes particular significance because the validity of Talb-i-Muwathibat is inextricably linked with the proof of first knowledge. Unless the source from which information regarding the sale reached the pre-emptor is satisfactorily proved through confidence inspiring evidence, it becomes impossible for the Court to determine whether the demand was made immediately upon receipt of information or after an unexplained delay. For ready reference, the exact words deposed by the deceased respondent/plaintiff as P.W.4 are reproduced in verbatim infra: 䆀 ۔䞈 ᮟ 䜫  ǖ ǔ̵ٳو ̵ǌ ǌ  ᜯوՙǎ ٶ 䗂 ۈ˄ǎٱ 〪 㤜 وا㦇 ز䅠 Ӓ ǔ  ٳو̵ǔ ǖ  䜫 ᮟ 䞈۔ ᜯوՙǎ ٶ ṵ 䗂 㭷 ۈ˄ǎٱ 〪 ارا⟤ 㪝⧋䮪 Ӓ ǔ ۔ 䆀  ƛ Ǖ Ɩ Ƈ ⸗وں ㈊۔ ㈀䐲 䆀 うᏡ ▧׏ǎ  䜫ں اور 䄎ى ز䅠 ଺ 㼋 䞈۔䞈 ዠ 㭷 〫 䗂 (underline for emphasis) This statement of P.W.4- original plaintiff when viewed in the light that Talb-i-Muwathibat implies to ‘jumping demand’/’immediate demand by a pre-emptor’, is found wanting, as Black's Law Dictionary, Eighth Edition on page 764 defines the word 'Immediate' to mean "occurring without delay; instant". In Webster Comprehensive Dictionary Encyclopaedic Edition on page 631 the word ‘immediate' has been defined to mean "without delay; instant."

In addition to the above, the informer could not disclose as to how he received information about the disputed transaction as the pleadings in this regard are silent. The law in this regard was comprehensively examined by this Court in Muhammad Riaz v. Muhammad Akram and others (2024 SCMR 692). The Court held that only a complete chain regarding the transmission of information concerning the sale can establish the essential ingredients of Talb-i-Muwathibat, namely: (i) the exact time, date and place at which the pre-emptor first acquired knowledge of the sale; and (ii) the immediate declaration of intention by the pre- emptor to exercise the right of pre-emption. The Court further held that where the source from whom the informer acquired the information remains unproved, the entire foundation of Talb-i- Muwathibat becomes doubtful and the claim for pre-emption cannot succeed.

Similar observations were made in Farid Ullah Khan (supra), wherein it was emphasized that proof of first knowledge is not a peripheral matter but goes to the very root of the claim. Since the law requires the pre-emptor to react immediately upon learning of the sale, the Court must first be satisfied regarding the precise circumstances in which such information was received. Unless the source of information is proved through a complete and unbroken chain, the Court cannot safely conclude that the statutory requirement of immediacy has been fulfilled.

Pursuant to the above, the respondents pleaded that the original pre-emptor acquired knowledge of the impugned sale through Javed Hussain in the presence of Karam Hussain and thereupon performed Talb-i-Muwathibat. However, a careful examination of the evidence reveals that the respondents failed to establish the complete chain through which information regarding the sale allegedly reached the pre-emptor. The record is conspicuously silent regarding the source from whom the alleged informer himself acquired knowledge of the transaction. No satisfactory evidence was produced to establish how, when and through whom information concerning the sale travelled before reaching the pre-emptor.

More importantly, the evidence led by the respondents is not free from material contradictions on matters going to the root of the controversy. The version appearing in the plaint does not fully correspond with the testimony subsequently brought on record. The witnesses have made statements regarding the alleged gathering, the persons present therein, the circumstances in which information was conveyed and the performance of Talb-i- Muwathibat which are not entirely consistent with one another. Some witnesses have introduced facts not pleaded, while others have omitted facts that constitute the very foundation of the respondents' case.

Likewise, material discrepancies also emerge from the evidence of the respondents' witnesses regarding the alleged Majlis, the identity of persons present at the relevant time and the precise manner in which the information regarding the sale was communicated to the pre-emptor. These contradictions are not minor discrepancies attributable to lapse of memory; rather, they relate to foundational facts upon which the entire claim of pre- emption rests.

We are mindful of the principle that every contradiction does not necessarily destroy a witness's credibility. However, where the right asserted is a weak and feeble right requiring strict compliance with statutory conditions, contradictions touching upon the source of information, the constitution of the Majlis, the identity of witnesses to the demand and the circumstances surrounding the performance of Talb-i-Muwathibat cannot be brushed aside as inconsequential. Such contradictions strike at the very foundation of the claim and render the evidence unsafe for sustaining a decree for pre-emption.

The learned High Court, while affirming the findings regarding performance of Talbs, failed to undertake a meaningful examination of these material inconsistencies. Rather than scrutinizing whether the respondents had discharged the strict burden cast upon them by law, the learned High Court proceeded on the assumption that the issue already stood concluded by earlier findings. Such an approach, in our respectful view, overlooks the settled principle that a decree for pre-emption cannot be sustained unless every ingredient constituting the right is established through clear, consistent and trustworthy evidence.

We are, therefore, persuaded to hold that the respondents failed to establish the complete chain through which information regarding the impugned sale reached the original pre-emptor. The evidence led in support of Talb-i-Muwathibat is further rendered doubtful by material contradictions affecting the core of the respondents' case. Consequently, the finding recorded by the Courts below regarding valid performance of Talb-i-Muwathibat cannot be sustained.

Since learned counsel for the respondents has argued that Talb-i-Ishhad was independently proved through the issuance of notices, we shall now examine whether the respondents succeeded in establishing valid performance of Talb-i-Ishhad in accordance with the requirements of law.

Even if the respondents were to overcome the deficiencies noted above regarding Talb-i-Muwathibat, they were further required to establish strict compliance with the requirements governing Talb-i-Ishhad. Under section 13(3) of the Punjab Pre- emption Act, 1991, the pre-emptor is obliged, after making Talb-i- Muwathibat, to affirm and confirm his intention to exercise the right of pre-emption by making Talb-i-Ishhad in the presence of two truthful witnesses and by serving notice upon the vendee in the manner recognized by law. Since Talb-i-Ishhad constitutes a statutory safeguard designed to provide formal and timely notice to the vendee regarding the assertion of the right of pre-emption, its performance and proof must also satisfy the strict requirements laid down by law.

The legal position stands authoritatively settled by this Court in Sardar Muhammad (deceased) (supra), wherein it was held that service of notice relating to Talb-i-Ishhad upon the vendee is a mandatory requirement and that failure to prove performance of even one Talb is sufficient to defeat the entire claim. Similar principles were reiterated in Mir Muhammad Khan and others v. Haider and others (PLD 2020 SC 233), wherein a five-member Bench of this Court held that where service of notice is denied, the burden squarely lies upon the pre-emptor to prove such service through legally admissible evidence. Mere dispatch of a notice does not constitute proof of service.

Earlier, in Bashir Ahmed v. Ghulam Rasool (2011 SCMR 762), this Court held that where service of notice is disputed, the pre- emptor must establish actual service through reliable evidence, including, where necessary, the testimony of the concerned postal official. Likewise, in Munawar Hussain v. Afaq Ahmed (2013 SCMR 721), it was held that service upon one vendee cannot be treated as service upon another and that strict proof of service upon every vendee is required. More recently, in Sherzali and others v. Saad Ullah Khan (Civil Appeal No.888 of 2020), this Court once again emphasized that every requirement relating to Talbs must be observed with utmost strictness.

The rationale underlying the above authorities is self-evident. Since the right of pre-emption seeks to defeat an otherwise valid transfer of property, the law insists that the vendee must receive clear and timely notice regarding the assertion of such right. Consequently, proof of dispatch alone is not enough; what must be established is service in the manner contemplated by law. Where service is denied, the burden remains upon the pre-emptor throughout and any deficiency in proof operates against him.

In the present case, serious doubts arise not only regarding proof of service but also regarding the validity of the Talb-i-Ishhad itself. Learned counsel for the appellant has rightly pointed out that the notice relied upon by the respondents does not clearly disclose the affirmation and confirmation of the intention to exercise the right of pre-emption in the manner contemplated by section 13(3) of the Act. More importantly, once the very making of Talb-i-Muwathibat becomes doubtful, the subsequent Talb-i-Ishhad necessarily loses its legal foundation. As held in Farid Ullah Khan (supra), Talb-i- Muwathibat is the foundation upon which the entire superstructure of the claim rests; where the foundation collapses, the superstructure cannot survive.

We have already concluded that the respondents failed to establish a valid Talb-i-Muwathibat and failed to prove the complete chain of information leading to the alleged first knowledge of the sale. In such circumstances, examination of the second Talb becomes largely academic. Nevertheless, even independently viewed, the evidence led by the respondents falls short of the strict standard required for proving Talb-i-Ishhad. We are, therefore, unable to sustain the concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below on this aspect of the matter.

It is also necessary to deal with one aspect of the impugned judgment which materially influenced the approach adopted by the learned High Court. A careful reading of the impugned judgment reveals that although the learned High Court undertook an independent appraisal of the evidence while examining the question of the appellant's alleged co-sharership, it declined to subject the evidence relating to Talb-i-Muwathibat and Talb-i-Ishhad to the same degree of scrutiny, principally on the premise that the findings recorded by the learned trial Court on those issues had attained finality. The correctness of this approach necessarily calls for an examination of the scope and ambit of the High Court's revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. It is a well settled principle of law that where the judgments of the Courts below are at variance, or where the findings recorded by them suffer from misreading or non-reading of material evidence resulting in miscarriage of justice, the High Court, while exercising revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, is not merely empowered but is under a duty to re-examine the evidence and determine which of the conflicting views is in accordance with the record and the law. The contours of such jurisdiction were delineated by this Court in G.M. Sikdar v. The Controller of Import And Export and 2 Others (PLD 1970 SC 158) and Mollah Ejahar Ali v. Government of East Pakistan (PLD 1970 SC 173), wherein it was held that interference in revision is warranted where the findings of the Courts below are vitiated by material irregularity or misreading of evidence resulting in failure of justice. The same principle was reiterated in Shaukat Nawaz v. Muhammad Siddique (1988 SCMR 851), and subsequently applied in Abdul Rashid v. Muhammad Yaseen and another (2010 SCMR 1871), wherein this Court held that in such circumstances it becomes the duty and obligation of the High Court to re-examine the evidence and interfere in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. Likewise, in Amir Haider v. Shabir Ahmad through Legal Heirs and others (2000 SCMR 859), this Court recognized that the High Court is competent to reverse the findings of the lower appellate Court where the same are the result of misreading or non-reading of material evidence. The principle was further elaborated in Qutab Din and another v. Muhammad Ashraf and others (2005 SCMR 1103), wherein this Court approved the High Court's observation that, since the judgments of the Courts below were at variance, it had become incumbent upon it to appraise the entire evidence to ascertain which judgment correctly reflected the record. Similar was the view taken in Karim Bakhsh through L.Rs. and others v. Jindwadda Shah and others (2005 SCMR 1518), wherein this Court held that where the subordinate Courts had returned divergent conclusions, the High Court was fully justified in appreciating the evidence afresh and arriving at its own independent conclusion. The legal position emerging from the aforesaid authorities admits of no ambiguity: where conflicting findings are before the High Court, or where the findings suffer from material irregularity occasioned by misreading or non-reading of evidence, the High Court is duty-bound to undertake an independent appraisal of the record so as to determine which of the competing judgments is legally sustainable. In the present case, although the learned High Court undertook such an exercise while examining the question of the appellant's alleged co- sharership, it inexplicably declined to do so in relation to the validity of Talb-i-Muwathibat and Talb-i-Ishhad by erroneously treating the findings of the learned trial Court on those issues as having attained finality. Such a selective exercise of revisional jurisdiction is contrary to the settled principles repeatedly laid down by this Court.

Once it is accepted that the learned High Court possessed ample jurisdiction and, in appropriate cases, was under an obligation to independently reappraise the evidence where the judgments of the Courts below were at variance or suffered from misreading or non-reading of material evidence, the only question that survives is whether the learned High Court was justified in declining to undertake such an exercise on the ground that no cross-objections had been filed against the findings recorded by the learned trial Court regarding the performance of Talbs. The answer, in our considered view, must be returned in the negative. In Shahro and others v. Mst. Fatima and others (PLD 1998 SC 1512), this Court authoritatively explained the distinction between challenging a decree and supporting a decree. It was held that a respondent, without filing cross-objections, is fully entitled to support a decree on any ground available on the record, including a ground decided against him by the Court below. The requirement of cross-objections arises only where a party seeks to attack or vary the decree itself. This Court further emphasized that the powers conferred upon an appellate Court under Order XLI Rule 33, C.P.C. are sufficiently wide to enable it to pass such decree or order as ought to have been passed in the circumstances of the case, notwithstanding the absence of any appeal or cross-objections.

More recently, in Mushtaq-ul-Aarifeen and others v. Mumtaz Muhammad and others (2022 SCMR 55), this Court reiterated that an appeal is a continuation of the original proceedings and that an appellate Court is under an obligation to reconsider the controversy afresh, both on facts and law. It was further held that failure to file cross-objections does not preclude a party from canvassing a question of law before the appellate forum, nor does it divest the appellate Court of jurisdiction to examine and determine such question. This Court expressly observed that the appellate Court may even grant relief in favour of a party who has neither preferred an appeal nor filed cross-objections, if the circumstances of the case so require.

In the present case, the appellant consistently questioned the legality of the respondents' claim for pre-emption and specifically assailed the findings relating to the performance of Talbs. The issue, therefore, was very much alive before the learned High Court. More importantly, the questions relating to Talb-i-Muwathibat and Talb- i-Ishhad were not collateral or subsidiary matters but constituted the very foundation of the respondents' entitlement to a decree for pre-emption. Once the decree passed by the learned appellate Court was under challenge, the learned High Court was under a duty to examine whether the mandatory statutory requirements governing the exercise of the right of pre-emption had in fact been satisfied.

The learned High Court, however, declined to undertake such examination by treating the findings regarding Talbs as having attained finality. In doing so, it overlooked the settled distinction between assailing a decree and supporting a decree on alternative grounds and further failed to exercise the jurisdiction vested in it to determine whether the respondents had established the foundational requirements of their claim. The impugned approach cannot be sustained in view of the principles laid down by this Court in Shahro (supra) and Mushtaq-ul-Aarifeen (supra).

Consequently, we have independently examined the pleadings and evidence relating to Talb-i-Muwathibat and Talb-i-Ishhad and, for the reasons already recorded, have found that the respondents failed to establish the mandatory requirements prescribed by law. The contrary view adopted by the learned High Court is, therefore, unsustainable.

The cumulative effect of the foregoing discussion is that the respondents failed to establish the mandatory ingredients necessary for the successful enforcement of the right of pre-emption. The respondents failed to establish the complete chain through which information regarding the sale reached the original pre-emptor. The evidence relating to the alleged Majlis and performance of Talbs is marred by material contradictions touching upon the very foundation of the claim. Furthermore, valid performance of Talb-i- Ishhad has also not been established in the manner required by law. The learned High Court, while affirming the decree in favour of the respondents, failed to appreciate these fundamental deficiencies and consequently fell into legal error.

Since the respondents failed to establish valid performance of Talb-i-Muwathibat, the very foundation of the suit falls. As repeatedly held by this Court, where the first Talb is not proved in accordance with law, the entire superstructure of the claim for pre- emption collapses. The respondents were, therefore, not entitled to a decree for possession through pre-emption.

For what has been discussed above, this appeal is allowed. The judgment dated 13.06.2019 passed by the learned Lahore High Court, Rawalpindi Bench, in Civil Revisions Nos.315-D and 360-D of 2010, as well as the judgment and decree dated 13.03.2010 passed by the learned first appellate Court, are set aside. Consequently, the judgment and decree dated 01.12.2006 passed by the learned trial Court dismissing the suit are restored, albeit for reasons different from those recorded by the learned trial Court. There shall be no order as to the costs. C.P.L.A.No.3740/2019

C.P.L.A.No.3740/2019 arising out of the same impugned judgment and involving identical questions of fact and law, was heard together with the present appeal. Since the issues raised therein stand fully covered by the reasons recorded above, the said petition is disposed of in the same terms. JUDGE JUDGE JUDGE Announced in open Court on13.07.2026.
